Lordly
LORD-lee
adj. (befitting a lord; magnificent — used once, of the dish in which Jael brought Sisera butter)
From Old English hlaford, the loaf-ward, the keeper of the bread. At Judges 5:25 it renders Hebrew addir, majestic or noble, describing the vessel — the AV's only use of the adjective.

Biblical Definition

Deborah's song slows down over a single domestic detail: He asked water, and she gave him milk; she brought forth butter in a lordly dish. Sisera, captain of nine hundred chariots of iron, asks for water at a tent door and is given better than he asked — curds, in the best vessel in the house. Everything in the line is hospitality, and every bit of it is a trap. The lordly dish is the last courtesy he receives; the next verse has the workman's hammer and the nail. The song is not sentimental about Jael and does not pretend the deed was gentle, but it pronounces her blessed above women, because the man at the tent door was the standing enemy of the covenant people and the LORD had already said He would sell Sisera into the hand of a woman.

The word is worth keeping because of what the New Testament does with the idea behind it. Lordly is the adjective of one who is over, and the apostles forbid it inside the church with unusual sharpness. Peter charges the elders to feed the flock, Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock; our Lord says the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion, but it shall not be so among you. There is a lordly dish in the tent of Jael and there is a lordly manner in the house of God, and Scripture blesses the first and forbids the second.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): becoming a lord; magnificent; hence also proud, haughty, imperious — both senses in the one word.

expand to see more

LORDLY, a. Becoming a lord; pertaining to a lord; proud; haughty; imperious; insolent.

LORD, n. A master; a person possessing supreme power and authority; a ruler; a governor.

BUTTER, n. An oily substance obtained from cream or milk by churning.

DISH, n. A broad open vessel, made of various materials, used for serving up meat and various kinds of food at the table.

MAGNIFICENT, a. Grand in appearance; splendid; pompous; displaying greatness of size or extent.

Key Scripture

Judges 5:25 — "He asked water, and she gave him milk; she brought forth butter in a lordly dish."

Judges 5:24 — "Blessed above women shall Jael the wife of Heber the Kenite be, blessed shall she be above women in the tent."

Judges 5:26 — "She put her hand to the nail, and her right hand to the workmen's hammer; and with the hammer she smote Sisera, she smote off his head, when she had pierced and stricken through his temples."

1 Peter 5:3 — "Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock."

Modern Corruption

Lordly bearing is the standing temptation of church office, and the New Testament names it directly rather than leaving it to good manners.

expand to see more

The eldership is the one place in the world where a man is given real authority and told in the same breath that he may not carry it like an authority. Peter's prohibition is blunt — not as being lords over God's heritage — and the reason is given immediately: the flock is God's, not the shepherd's, and the chief Shepherd is coming. Every domineering pastorate in history has been built on a quiet inversion of that sentence. Where the plurality of elders is thinned to one strong man, where the congregation may not question, where the pulpit is used to settle personal scores, the lordly manner has taken hold whatever the constitution says.

The corresponding error is to hear Peter as forbidding authority itself. He does not. He charges the elders to feed, to take the oversight, and he tells the younger to submit themselves to the elder — real office, real rule, real obedience. What is forbidden is the manner of the Gentile princes, who exercise dominion because dominion is what they have. The alternative Peter names is not weakness but example: being ensamples to the flock, a man who leads by going first into the obedience he asks for, which costs a good deal more than issuing it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew addir (H117), majestic, noble, excellent; sephel (H5602), a bowl or dish; Greek katakurieuo (G2634), to lord it over.

expand to see more

Hebrew addir (H117) — majestic, noble; used of the LORD Himself in Psalm 8, and here of a bowl.

Hebrew sephel (H5602) — a bowl or basin; the vessel Jael chose for the last courtesy Sisera received.

Hebrew chemah (H2529) — curd, butter; richer than the water he asked for.

Greek katakurieuo (G2634) — to exercise dominion over; forbidden to elders in 1 Peter 5:3.

Greek tupos (G5179) — a pattern, an ensample; the alternative Peter sets against lordly rule.

Usage

"“she brought forth butter in a lordly dish” — the last courtesy before the hammer."

"“Blessed above women shall Jael... be” — the song's verdict on the tent."

"“Neither as being lords over God's heritage” — the manner forbidden to elders."
